title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years later, and the Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her.
hook: Ancient Egypt was already ancient to the ancient Egyptians.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford was underway by 1096. The Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
hook: "Old" and "new" world timelines overlap in surprising ways.

title: The shortest war lasted under an hour
body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment. The Sultan's palace was wrecked and a pro-British ruler installed.
hook: Power gaps can make conflicts brutally brief.

title: Napoleon was not unusually short
body: He was about 5 feet 7 inches, average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth grew from confusion between French and English inches and from British cartoons mocking him.
hook: Propaganda can outlive the person it targets.

title: The Great Fire of London had few recorded deaths
body: The 1666 fire destroyed around 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the true toll among the poor was higher but went uncounted.
hook: Who gets counted shapes what history remembers.

title: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
body: No horned helmet has been found from a Viking-age warrior grave. The image comes largely from 19th-century art and costume design, including Wagner's opera productions.
hook: Much of our picture of the past is Victorian stagecraft.

title: The printing press spread faster than you would think
body: Gutenberg printed his Bible around 1455. By 1500, presses operated in more than 250 European towns and had produced millions of books.
hook: New information technology has always spread fast.

title: Ancient Romans used a kind of concrete that lasts
body: Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash. Some harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of seawater, and researchers think minerals growing inside the concrete help seal cracks.
hook: Old techniques can still teach modern engineers.

title: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
body: The conflict between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453. It was a series of wars broken by truces, not one continuous fight.
hook: Historians name periods after the fact, not neatly.

title: Tsar Peter the Great taxed beards
body: In 1698 Peter imposed a tax on beards to push Russian nobles towards Western European fashion. Payers carried a token proving they had paid.
hook: Rulers have long used taxes to change behaviour.

title: The Black Death killed around a third of Europe
body: Between 1347 and 1351 plague swept Europe, killing an estimated 30 to 50 percent of the population. Labour shortages afterwards pushed up wages for surviving workers.
hook: Catastrophes can shift economic power.

title: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary
body: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it had a 20-year permit. It was saved partly because it proved useful as a radio transmission tower.
hook: Usefulness is a strong defence against demolition.

title: Ancient Olympians competed naked
body: In the ancient Greek Games, male athletes competed nude. The word "gymnasium" comes from the Greek "gymnos", meaning naked.
hook: Words carry fossils of old customs.

title: The Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs
body: Found in 1799, the stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek. Jean-François Champollion used it to announce his decipherment in 1822.
hook: One translated text can open a whole lost language.

title: Mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built
body: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid was built around 4,500 years ago.
hook: Extinction is often a slow fade, not a single event.

title: The first known strike was in ancient Egypt
body: Around 1157 BC, tomb builders at Deir el-Medina stopped work because their grain rations were late. Records of the protest survive on papyrus.
hook: Workers have bargained over pay for over 3,000 years.

title: The Library of Alexandria declined slowly
body: There was no single fire that destroyed everything. The library faded over centuries through funding cuts, political purges and several conflicts.
hook: Institutions usually die from neglect, not drama.

title: Sliced bread was briefly banned in the US
body: In January 1943 the US banned sliced bread to save resources during the war. Public outcry got the ban lifted within about two months.
hook: Small comforts can carry big political weight.

title: Medieval people did not think the Earth was flat
body: Educated Europeans in the Middle Ages generally knew the Earth was round. The flat-Earth myth about them was popularised in the 1800s.
hook: Each era likes to think the last was more ignorant.

title: The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon
body: It is very long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts have confirmed it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
hook: Big claims deserve a quick check.

title: Coffee houses were nicknamed penny universities
body: In 17th-century England, a penny bought entry and coffee, plus hours of debate and news. Lloyd's of London began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house.
hook: Shared spaces can incubate whole industries.

title: Paper money started in China
body: China was using paper money by the Song dynasty in the 11th century. Europe did not adopt banknotes widely until the 1600s.
hook: Many "modern" inventions are centuries old.

title: The Titanic's sister ship had a long career
body: RMS Olympic, Titanic's near-identical sister, served from 1911 to 1935. She was nicknamed "Old Reliable" and even rammed a German U-boat in 1918.
hook: Fame often goes to the disaster, not the success.

title: The Aztec capital was built on a lake
body: Tenochtitlan stood on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways. Mexico City sits on the drained lakebed and is sinking as a result.
hook: Cities inherit the choices of their founders.

title: The Romans had fast food counters
body: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, street counters serving hot food and drink. Many Romans in cramped flats had no kitchen of their own.
hook: Eating out is as old as city living.

title: The ancient Greeks had a vending machine
body: Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated device in the first century AD. A coin dropped onto a lever released a measured amount of holy water.
hook: Clever automation is older than electricity.

title: Cats were sacred in ancient Egypt
body: Egyptians linked cats with the goddess Bastet. Killing one, even by accident, could bring severe punishment, and many cats were mummified.
hook: What a culture protects reveals what it values.

title: The first speeding ticket was for 8 mph
body: In 1896 Walter Arnold was fined in Kent for driving at about 8 mph, four times the limit of 2 mph in town. A man with a flag was supposed to walk ahead of cars.
hook: Every new technology outpaces its rules.

title: Queen Victoria's reign was not the longest British reign
body: Victoria reigned for 63 years. Elizabeth II overtook her in 2015 and reigned for 70 years.
hook: Records are made to be broken, eventually.

title: The Spanish flu probably did not start in Spain
body: Spain was neutral in the First World War and reported the 1918 flu openly. Countries at war censored news, so it looked like Spain was hit first.
hook: Who reports a story can shape its name.

title: Ancient Romans used urine to clean clothes
body: Urine contains ammonia, which helps lift grease and dirt. Laundries called fullonicae collected it from public pots, and it was even taxed.
hook: Yesterday's waste was someone's raw material.

title: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France
body: It was designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi and dedicated in 1886. Gustave Eiffel's company engineered its internal iron framework.
hook: Friendship between nations can be cast in copper.

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
body: It is covered in copper, which was originally a shiny reddish-brown. Over about 20 years, weathering turned it green.
hook: Time changes even monuments.

title: Ancient Egyptians used stone pillows
body: Wealthier Egyptians slept with their heads on curved headrests made of wood or stone. They raised the head and may have kept insects away.
hook: Comfort is shaped by climate and culture.

title: The first Olympic marathon winner was a water carrier
body: Spyridon Louis won the marathon at the 1896 Athens Olympics. He became a national hero in Greece.
hook: Ordinary people can make extraordinary history.

title: London's Big Ben is a bell, not the tower
body: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
hook: Nicknames often stick to the wrong thing.

title: Medieval castles were often colourful
body: Many castle walls were whitewashed or painted, and interiors were bright with colour. We picture them grey because the paint has worn away.
hook: Ruins hide how vivid the past was.

title: The Mayflower later became a barn, some say
body: A popular story claims the Mayflower's timbers were reused in a barn in Buckinghamshire. Historians consider the link possible but unproven.
hook: Not every good story can be verified.

title: Abacus users can still beat calculators
body: Skilled abacus users can do arithmetic extremely fast. In a 1946 contest in Tokyo, an abacus user beat an electric calculator in most rounds.
hook: Practised skill can rival machines.

title: The Romans did not use the number zero
body: Roman numerals have no symbol for zero. The concept of zero as a number came from India and spread through the Arab world.
hook: Some ideas are invented, not discovered.

title: Pirates rarely buried treasure
body: Most pirates spent or traded their loot quickly. The buried treasure idea was popularised by the novel Treasure Island in 1883.
hook: Fiction can shape how we imagine history.

title: Ancient Greek statues were painted
body: Traces of pigment show many Greek statues were brightly coloured. The pure white marble look we admire came later as paint wore off.
hook: The past was more colourful than we think.

title: The Leaning Tower of Pisa leaned during construction
body: Building began in 1173, and the tower started tilting before it was finished because of soft ground. Builders tried to compensate by making upper floors slightly taller on one side.
hook: Mistakes can become icons.

title: Before alarm clocks there were knocker-ups
body: In industrial Britain, people were paid to wake workers by tapping on windows with long poles or shooting peas at them.
hook: Every problem creates a job.

title: Lincoln was a licensed bartender
body: Abraham Lincoln co-owned a store in New Salem, Illinois, which got a licence to sell liquor in 1833.
hook: Leaders often have surprising early careers.

title: The first known map of the world is Babylonian
body: The Babylonian Map of the World, a clay tablet from around the 6th century BC, shows Babylon at the centre surrounded by water.
hook: Maps show beliefs as much as places.

title: The Ottoman Empire lasted over 600 years
body: Founded around 1299, it ended in 1922. At its peak it stretched across parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.
hook: Empires can last longer than nations exist today.

title: Silk was a closely guarded Chinese secret
body: For centuries China kept silk-making secret. Byzantine monks are said to have smuggled silkworm eggs to the West around 550 AD.
hook: Industrial secrets have always been worth stealing.

title: The Hanseatic League was a medieval trade network
body: From the 13th to 17th centuries, towns across northern Europe joined forces to protect trade. It controlled much of Baltic commerce.
hook: Cooperation can be as powerful as empire.

title: Tea was once used as money
body: In parts of Asia, compressed tea bricks were used as currency. They could be traded, or eaten and drunk if needed.
hook: Money is whatever people agree to accept.

title: The Gregorian calendar skipped days
body: When Catholic countries adopted it in 1582, 10 days were skipped. Britain switched in 1752 and skipped 11 days.
hook: Even time can be rearranged by decree.

title: Ancient Rome had a population of about a million
body: At its height around the 2nd century AD, Rome may have had up to a million people. No European city matched that again until London in the 1800s.
hook: Cities can shrink as well as grow.

title: The Battle of Hastings was not at Hastings
body: It was fought in 1066 about 10 kilometres away, at what is now the town of Battle. The abbey there marks the spot.
hook: Names drift from the places they describe.

title: The Magna Carta was mostly repealed
body: Of its original clauses, only three remain part of English law. Its lasting power is as a symbol of limits on power.
hook: Symbols can outlast the text behind them.

title: Thomas Edison did not invent the light bulb
body: Many inventors made electric lights before him. Edison's team made a practical, long-lasting bulb and a system to power it.
hook: Winning often means improving, not inventing.

title: The first photograph took hours to expose
body: Nicéphore Niépce's view from a window, made around 1826–27, needed an exposure of many hours, possibly days.
hook: Instant was once unimaginable.

title: Ancient Persians had refrigerators
body: Yakhchals were domed structures that stored ice through hot desert summers using shade, insulation and evaporation.
hook: Clever design can beat harsh climates.

title: Women in Britain first voted nationally in 1918
body: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave some women over 30 the vote. Equal voting with men came in 1928.
hook: Rights often arrive in stages.

title: Tutankhamun's tomb was found nearly intact
body: Howard Carter found it in 1922. Most Egyptian royal tombs had been robbed long before.
hook: Being forgotten can protect you.

title: The first email was sent in 1971
body: Ray Tomlinson sent it between two computers next to each other. He chose the @ sign to separate user and machine names.
hook: Big shifts can start with small tests.

title: The Inca kept records with knots
body: Quipu were cords with knots that recorded numbers and possibly other information. Experts still debate how much they could record.
hook: Writing is not the only way to remember.

title: Gladiators were not always fought to the death
body: Gladiators were expensive to train, and many bouts ended without a death. A defeated fighter could be spared.
hook: Spectacle and economics are often linked.

title: The Berlin Wall fell partly by mistake
body: On 9 November 1989, an East German spokesman wrongly said new travel rules applied immediately. Crowds gathered at the border, and guards opened the gates.
hook: History can turn on one confused announcement.

title: Ancient Mesopotamians invented the 60-minute hour
body: The Babylonians used a base-60 number system. That is why we have 60 seconds in a minute and 360 degrees in a circle.
hook: Old maths still runs our clocks.

title: Lady Godiva's ride may be a legend
body: The story of her riding naked through Coventry first appears long after her death. Historians doubt it happened.
hook: Legends can attach to real people.

title: The Great Stink pushed London to build sewers
body: In the hot summer of 1858, the stench from the Thames was so bad that Parliament acted. Joseph Bazalgette's sewers followed.
hook: Crisis can force overdue change.

title: The ancient Greeks invented the Olympics in 776 BC
body: The first recorded Games at Olympia had one event, a short foot race. More events were added over centuries.
hook: Big traditions can start small.

title: Chess was once played with different rules
body: The queen used to be a weak piece. Around 1475, rules in Spain made her the most powerful piece, speeding up the game.
hook: Games evolve to stay exciting.

title: The first vaccine came from cowpox
body: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox could protect against smallpox. The word vaccine comes from the Latin "vacca", meaning cow.
hook: Breakthroughs can come from careful observation.

title: Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated
body: The WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign. It had killed hundreds of millions.
hook: Global cooperation can end a plague.

title: The first postage stamp was the Penny Black
body: Issued in Britain in 1840, it let the sender prepay postage. Before, the receiver often paid.
hook: Small fixes can transform a system.

title: Ancient Egyptians invented toothpaste of a kind
body: They used mixtures that included powdered ox hooves, ashes and eggshells. It was rough but helped clean teeth.
hook: Hygiene is an ancient pursuit.

title: The longest-reigning monarch ruled 72 years
body: Louis XIV of France reigned from 1643 to 1715, starting at age four. He built the Palace of Versailles.
hook: Inheriting power young can mean holding it long.

title: Medieval monks invented a form of champagne, by legend
body: Dom Pérignon is often credited, but sparkling wine existed before him. He worked to improve wine quality.
hook: Credit often goes to the famous name.

title: Venice was built on wooden piles
body: Millions of wooden stakes driven into the mud support the city. Underwater and without oxygen, the wood has lasted for centuries.
hook: Hidden foundations hold up whole cities.

title: The Wright brothers' first flight lasted 12 seconds
body: On 17 December 1903, Orville Wright flew about 37 metres. Later that day Wilbur flew 260 metres in 59 seconds.
hook: The beginning of something huge can look tiny.

title: Ancient Rome had a central heating system
body: Wealthy Romans used the hypocaust, which circulated hot air under floors and inside walls.
hook: Comfort engineering has a long history.

title: The Taj Mahal took about 20 years to build
body: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered it in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Around 20,000 workers were involved.
hook: Grief can inspire great works.

title: The Domesday Book was a royal survey
body: In 1086 William the Conqueror ordered a survey of land and property across much of England. It recorded about 13,000 places.
hook: Governments have always wanted data.

title: The first British banknotes were handwritten
body: The Bank of England, founded in 1694, issued handwritten notes for specific amounts. Fully printed notes came later.
hook: Trust in paper had to be built.

title: Hadrian's Wall stretched coast to coast
body: Built from AD 122, it ran about 117 kilometres across northern England. It had forts, gates and watchtowers along its length.
hook: Borders have long been built in stone.

title: The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure for millennia
body: At about 146 metres originally, it was the tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years. Lincoln Cathedral's spire overtook it around 1311.
hook: Some records last almost forever.

title: Ancient Rome had a fire brigade
body: Emperor Augustus created the Vigiles in AD 6. They fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.
hook: Public services grow with cities.

title: The first public museum opened in Oxford
body: The Ashmolean Museum opened in 1683. It is often called Britain's first public museum.
hook: Knowledge became public property slowly.

title: Spartan boys started military training at seven
body: In ancient Sparta, boys entered the agoge, a tough state training programme. It shaped them into soldiers.
hook: Societies raise people for their priorities.

title: Ancient Chinese used dragon bones to find writing
body: In 1899, scholars noticed inscriptions on "dragon bones" sold as medicine. They were oracle bones, the earliest known Chinese writing.
hook: Treasure can hide in plain sight.

title: Honey never goes off
body: Honey is so low in water and so acidic that bacteria cannot grow in it. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still edible.
hook: The right chemistry beats any preservative.

title: Your body has more bacterial cells than you might think
body: Current estimates put the bacteria in and on a human body at roughly the same number as human cells, about 38 trillion. Most live in the gut.
hook: You are an ecosystem, not a single organism.

title: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
body: At its triple point, about 0.01°C and very low pressure, water exists as solid, liquid and gas at once. Scientists use it to calibrate thermometers.
hook: Everyday substances behave strangely at the edges.

title: Bananas are slightly radioactive
body: Bananas contain potassium, and a small fraction of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40. You would need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
hook: Dose, not presence, decides danger.

title: Glass is not a slow-moving liquid
body: Old church windows are often thicker at the bottom, but that comes from how medieval glass was made and fitted. At room temperature glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow visibly.
hook: A tidy explanation is not always the true one.

title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
body: A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to about 30,000°C. The surface of the Sun is roughly 5,500°C.
hook: Brief events can be astonishingly extreme.

title: Humans share about 60 percent of genes with bananas
body: Many basic cell functions use genes common to almost all living things. Roughly 60 percent of human genes have a recognisable counterpart in bananas.
hook: All life runs on a shared toolkit.

title: Sound travels faster in water than in air
body: Sound moves at about 343 metres per second in air and around 1,480 in water. Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometres.
hook: The medium shapes the message.

title: Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold
body: This is called the Mpemba effect, after a Tanzanian student who noticed it in 1963. Scientists still argue over when and why it happens.
hook: Simple questions can stay open for decades.

title: Your stomach gets a new lining every few days
body: Stomach acid is strong enough to damage tissue, so the cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days. Mucus adds another protective layer.
hook: Constant renewal is a survival strategy.

title: Diamonds and pencil lead are the same element
body: Both are pure carbon. In diamond the atoms form a rigid 3D lattice; in graphite they form flat sheets that slide over each other.
hook: Structure can matter more than ingredients.

title: Octopuses have three hearts
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Their blood is blue because it uses copper-based haemocyanin to carry oxygen.
hook: Evolution finds more than one way to solve a problem.

title: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes
body: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across. A teaspoon of that material would weigh around a billion tonnes or more.
hook: Matter can be crushed beyond imagination.

title: Your brain uses about a fifth of your energy
body: The brain is around 2 percent of body weight but uses roughly 20 percent of the energy you burn at rest. Thinking is expensive.
hook: Intelligence comes at a metabolic cost.

title: Penicillin was found by accident
body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish left out over a holiday. Turning it into a usable medicine took more than a decade of work by others.
hook: Discovery needs luck and long follow-through.

title: Some metals melt in your hand
body: Gallium melts at about 29.8°C, below body temperature. A spoon made of it would melt in hot tea.
hook: "Solid" depends on the temperature you live at.

title: Hiccups may be a leftover from our ancestors
body: One theory links hiccups to breathing reflexes in amphibian ancestors that gulped air and water. The jury is still out.
hook: Our bodies carry echoes of deep evolutionary history.

title: The human eye can detect a single photon
body: Experiments suggest people can sometimes sense a single photon in total darkness. Most of the time, though, the brain filters out such weak signals.
hook: Our senses are sharper than our attention.

title: Mercury thermometers were phased out for safety
body: Mercury is toxic, and broken thermometers could release vapour. Many countries have restricted mercury thermometers, replacing them with digital or alcohol ones.
hook: Safety often wins over tradition, slowly.

title: Air is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen
body: The air you breathe is about 78 percent nitrogen and only about 21 percent oxygen. The rest is mostly argon, with a tiny share of carbon dioxide.
hook: The obvious ingredient is often not the main one.

title: Fingerprints form before birth
body: Ridges on your fingertips form by around the 17th week of pregnancy. Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
hook: Small random differences make us unique.

title: Antibiotics do not work on viruses
body: Antibiotics target structures found in bacteria, such as cell walls. Viruses lack these, so colds and flu are not helped by antibiotics.
hook: The right tool depends on the right diagnosis.

title: Rainbows are actually full circles
body: From the ground, the horizon cuts off the lower half of a rainbow. From a plane you can sometimes see the full circle.
hook: Our viewpoint hides much of the picture.

title: Your bones are constantly being rebuilt
body: Cells in your skeleton break down old bone and lay down new bone all the time. Over about a decade, much of your skeleton is replaced.
hook: Even the solid parts of us are always changing.

title: Atoms are mostly empty space
body: If an atom's nucleus were the size of a marble, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny centre.
hook: Solid things are mostly nothing at all.

title: Your nose can tell apart a huge number of smells
body: A 2014 study suggested humans could distinguish over a trillion odours, though other scientists challenged the maths. Either way, it is far more than once thought.
hook: Our senses are underrated.

title: A single bolt of lightning carries huge energy
body: A typical lightning flash carries about a billion joules. But it lasts so briefly that capturing it is impractical.
hook: Power and usefulness are different things.

title: Earth's core is about as hot as the Sun's surface
body: Scientists estimate the inner core is around 5,200°C. It stays solid because of enormous pressure.
hook: Pressure can change how matter behaves.

title: Sweat itself has almost no smell
body: Body odour comes mostly from bacteria breaking down sweat on the skin. Fresh sweat is nearly odourless.
hook: The smell is the side effect, not the cause.

title: Light can bend around gravity
body: Massive objects like galaxies bend light passing nearby. Astronomers use this gravitational lensing to see even more distant objects.
hook: Gravity can act like a lens.

title: Your ears keep growing
body: Ears and noses appear to get larger with age, partly because cartilage and skin change over time.
hook: Bodies keep changing all life long.

title: Plants can be grown without soil
body: Hydroponics grows plants in water with dissolved nutrients. Many supermarket herbs and lettuces are grown this way.
hook: Soil is helpful, not essential.

title: Sunsets are red because of scattering
body: When the Sun is low, its light passes through more air. Blue light scatters away, leaving reds and oranges.
hook: The same physics makes the sky blue by day.

title: Some frogs can freeze solid and survive
body: The wood frog can have much of its body water freeze in winter. Glucose acts as antifreeze in its cells, and it thaws in spring.
hook: Life finds a way through extremes.

title: Your heart beats around 100,000 times a day
body: At about 70 beats per minute, that is roughly 2.5 billion beats in an average lifetime.
hook: Steady repetition adds up.

title: Water expands when it freezes
body: Most substances shrink as they solidify, but ice is less dense than water. That is why ice floats and pipes can burst.
hook: Exceptions to rules can shape whole planets.

title: Stars twinkle because of Earth's air
body: Moving layers of air bend starlight slightly. Planets twinkle less because they appear as tiny discs rather than points.
hook: What you see depends on what is in between.

title: Sharks existed before trees
body: Sharks appear in the fossil record over 400 million years ago. The first true trees evolved around 385 million years ago.
hook: Some designs are just very good.

title: Humans glow faintly
body: The body gives off a tiny amount of visible light from chemical reactions. It is about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see.
hook: There is more around us than we perceive.

title: DNA in one cell is about two metres long
body: Stretched out, the DNA in a single human cell would be roughly two metres long. It is packed tightly into a nucleus too small to see.
hook: Packing is a superpower.

title: Venus flytraps count
body: A Venus flytrap closes only when trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds. That avoids wasting energy on raindrops.
hook: Simple counting saves energy.

title: Some bacteria can eat plastic
body: In 2016 scientists in Japan found a bacterium that breaks down PET plastic. Researchers are studying its enzymes to speed up recycling.
hook: Nature adapts to what we leave behind.

title: You are taller in the morning
body: Discs in your spine compress during the day. You can be about a centimetre shorter by evening.
hook: Gravity works on you all day.

title: Most dust in homes is not dead skin
body: Studies suggest much household dust comes from outdoors, tracked in on shoes or blown in. Skin is part of it, but not most.
hook: Common facts deserve a second look.

title: Helium is running low on Earth
body: Helium is light enough to escape into space once released. Most is collected from natural gas fields, and supplies are limited.
hook: Even the most common element in stars can be scarce here.

title: Electric eels can produce 600 volts
body: They use special cells called electrocytes, stacked like batteries. The shock stuns prey and deters predators.
hook: Biology invented batteries first.

title: Your brain cannot feel pain
body: The brain has no pain receptors, so surgeons can operate while patients are awake. Headaches come from surrounding tissues.
hook: The organ that feels everything feels nothing itself.

title: Earth is not a perfect sphere
body: It bulges at the equator because of its spin. The diameter at the equator is about 43 kilometres larger than pole to pole.
hook: Spin shapes planets.

title: Pure water does not conduct electricity well
body: Dissolved salts and minerals make water conductive. Very pure water is a poor conductor.
hook: It is the impurities that carry the current.

title: The placebo effect can be real
body: Patients given inactive treatments sometimes report genuine improvements, especially in pain. Expectations can change how the body responds.
hook: Belief has measurable effects.

title: The speed of light is a cosmic speed limit
body: Nothing with mass can reach light speed. At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light could circle Earth over seven times in a second.
hook: Some limits are built into physics.

title: Kidney stones can come from too little water
body: Not drinking enough lets minerals concentrate in urine and form crystals. Staying hydrated is a key prevention.
hook: Simple habits prevent painful problems.

title: Gold is mostly from colliding stars
body: Many heavy elements, including gold, are thought to form when neutron stars collide. The gold in jewellery may be older than the Earth.
hook: You may be wearing stardust.

title: Your skin is your largest organ
body: For an adult, skin covers around two square metres. It protects, regulates temperature and senses the world.
hook: The outside of you is an organ too.

title: Ants can lift many times their body weight
body: Some ants can carry objects many times heavier than themselves. Their small size makes this easier than it would be for large animals.
hook: Strength scales strangely with size.

title: Carbon dating has a limit
body: Radiocarbon dating works on organic material up to about 50,000 years old. After that, too little carbon-14 remains to measure.
hook: Every tool has a range.

title: Your gut has its own nervous system
body: The enteric nervous system has hundreds of millions of neurons. It can run digestion with little input from the brain.
hook: There is a second brain in your belly, of sorts.

title: Snowflakes are not all unique, technically
body: Simple tiny snow crystals can look identical. Large, complex snowflakes are almost certainly all different.
hook: The truth often depends on the detail.

title: Mosquitoes find you partly by your breath
body: They detect carbon dioxide from many metres away, then use heat and smell to close in.
hook: Breathing gives you away.

title: Cooking may have helped make our brains bigger
body: Some scientists argue cooking made food easier to digest, freeing energy for brain growth. It remains a debated theory.
hook: Technology may have shaped our biology.

title: Saliva starts digestion
body: An enzyme in saliva, amylase, begins breaking down starch in your mouth. Chew bread long enough and it starts to taste sweet.
hook: Digestion starts before you swallow.

title: Blue whales have hearts the size of a small car
body: A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kilograms. Its heartbeat can be detected from kilometres away.
hook: Size changes everything.

title: Rust is slow burning
body: Rusting and burning are both reactions with oxygen. Rust happens slowly; fire happens fast and releases heat and light.
hook: Same chemistry, different speed.

title: Your eyes see upside down
body: The lens of your eye projects an upside-down image onto the retina. Your brain flips it the right way up.
hook: Perception is partly construction.

title: Bones are stronger than steel by weight
body: Gram for gram, bone can be stronger than some steels. It is light, flexible and constantly repaired.
hook: Living materials can rival engineered ones.

title: Tears differ by cause
body: Scientists distinguish basal, reflex and emotional tears. Their chemical make-up varies.
hook: Even tears have types.

title: Some trees are thousands of years old
body: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California is over 4,800 years old. It was already old when the pyramids were built.
hook: Slow and steady can last millennia.

title: A day on Earth is getting longer
body: Tidal friction from the Moon is slowing Earth's spin. Days lengthen by about 1.8 milliseconds per century.
hook: Even time is changing.

title: The appendix may have a purpose
body: It was long thought useless, but some research suggests it stores helpful gut bacteria. The question is still being studied.
hook: Calling something useless can be premature.

title: Microwaves heat water molecules
body: Microwave ovens make water molecules vibrate, producing heat. Food with more water heats faster.
hook: Invisible waves do everyday work.

title: Yawning may cool the brain
body: One theory says yawning brings in cooler air to regulate brain temperature. Why yawns are contagious is still debated.
hook: Common behaviours can still be mysteries.

title: The Dead Sea lets you float
body: Its water is about ten times saltier than the ocean. The high density pushes swimmers up.
hook: Density decides what sinks.

title: Sound can break glass
body: If a sound matches a glass's natural resonant frequency and is loud enough, the vibrations can shatter it.
hook: The right frequency beats raw force.

title: Cows produce methane mostly by burping
body: Microbes in a cow's stomach produce methane as they digest grass. Most is released through burps, not the other end.
hook: Details matter in climate science.

title: Diamonds can burn
body: Heat a diamond to around 700–900°C with oxygen and it will burn, turning into carbon dioxide.
hook: Forever is relative.

title: Your fingernails grow faster than toenails
body: Fingernails grow around 3 millimetres a month. Toenails grow more slowly, roughly a third as fast.
hook: Different parts age at different speeds.

title: Lobster blood is colourless until exposed to air
body: It contains copper-based haemocyanin, which turns blue when it binds with oxygen.
hook: Colour can be a chemical signal.

title: Light from distant stars may be very old
body: Some stars we see are thousands of light years away. Their light left them thousands of years ago.
hook: Looking up is looking back.

title: Ice can be one of many types
body: Scientists have identified around 20 different forms of solid water. Most only exist at extreme pressures.
hook: Even familiar substances have hidden variety.

title: Fireflies make cold light
body: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction that wastes almost no energy as heat.
hook: Nature built efficient lighting long ago.

title: Tomatoes are botanically fruit
body: Botanically, a fruit develops from a flower and contains seeds. Tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers all qualify.
hook: Kitchen and science categories differ.

title: Laughing is contagious for a reason
body: Hearing laughter activates brain regions that prepare us to laugh too. It may help bond groups together.
hook: Shared emotion is social glue.

title: Your sense of smell is linked to memory
body: Smell signals travel close to brain areas for memory and emotion. That is why a scent can bring back a vivid moment.
hook: Memory has a nose.

title: The world's oldest company ran for over 1,400 years
body: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple builder, was founded in 578 AD. It traded independently until 2006, when it was absorbed by a larger construction firm.
hook: Longevity comes from doing one thing well for a very long time.

title: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicine
body: In 1886 pharmacist John Pemberton sold Coca-Cola in Atlanta as a tonic at soda fountains. It became a mass-market drink through marketing, not medicine.
hook: Products often find their real market by accident.

title: Nokia started as a paper mill
body: Nokia was founded in Finland in 1865 as a pulp mill. Over the next century it moved into rubber, cables and finally mobile phones.
hook: Companies can reinvent themselves many times.

title: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
body: On 26 June 1974, a pack of Wrigley's gum was the first product scanned by a UPC barcode at a supermarket in Ohio.
hook: Huge systems often start with a humble test.

title: Post-it Notes came from a failed glue
body: A 3M scientist created a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968 that nobody could find a use for. Years later a colleague used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his hymn book.
hook: A failure in one context can be a hit in another.

title: Supermarkets put milk at the back for a reason
body: Essentials like milk are often placed at the far end of the store so shoppers pass more products on the way. Each extra aisle is another chance to buy.
hook: Store layouts are designed, not accidental.

title: The 80/20 rule started with peas
body: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that 20 percent of the pea pods in his garden produced most of the peas. He then found that about 20 percent of people owned 80 percent of land in Italy.
hook: Uneven distributions show up everywhere.

title: Prices ending in 99 really work
body: Studies find that prices like £4.99 often sell better than £5.00 because shoppers anchor on the first digit. This is called the left-digit effect.
hook: Small framing changes move big decisions.

title: Lego nearly went bankrupt in 2003
body: After expanding into too many products, Lego faced heavy losses. It recovered by refocusing on its core bricks and cutting complexity.
hook: Focus can rescue a company that sprawled.

title: Amazon started as an online bookshop
body: When it launched in 1995, Amazon sold only books. Books were easy to ship and had a huge catalogue no physical store could stock.
hook: Start narrow, then expand.

title: Monopoly was originally a warning about landlords
body: The game began as The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show how land ownership concentrated wealth. Later versions dropped the message.
hook: Ideas can be repackaged to mean the opposite.

title: The first credit card was for restaurants
body: Diners Club launched in 1950 as a card for paying at restaurants in New York. It was a charge card, paid off in full each month.
hook: Big financial products often start in one niche.

title: Free shipping thresholds raise basket size
body: Many shoppers add items just to reach a free delivery threshold. Retailers set the line slightly above the typical order.
hook: Thresholds nudge behaviour more than discounts.

title: The decoy effect sells more large drinks
body: When a medium option priced close to the large is added, more people choose the large. The middle option exists mainly to make the big one look good value.
hook: Options can be designed to steer a choice.

title: Netflix once mailed DVDs
body: Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD-by-post rental service. It started streaming in 2007 and kept mailing discs until 2023.
hook: The winning business model may grow inside the old one.

title: The stock market's opening bell is a real bell
body: The New York Stock Exchange rings a bell to open and close trading each weekday. Guests ring it as a publicity event.
hook: Rituals help markets feel orderly.

title: Compound interest is called the eighth wonder
body: Money growing at 7 percent a year doubles roughly every 10 years. Starting earlier matters more than starting bigger.
hook: Time is the most powerful input.

title: Most new restaurants struggle in their first years
body: Studies of restaurant openings find a large share close within the first few years. Thin margins and high fixed costs leave little room for error.
hook: Passion needs a business model behind it.

title: Logos rarely use purple
body: Purple is among the least common main colours in big-brand logos; blue and red dominate. Colour choices signal trust, energy or luxury.
hook: Colour is part of the message.

title: Shipping containers changed world trade
body: Standard steel containers, introduced in 1956, cut the cost and time of loading ships dramatically. Global trade grew as a result.
hook: A boring standard can transform an industry.

title: The paperclip has a surprisingly rich history
body: The familiar double-loop Gem paperclip appeared in Britain in the 1870s and was never patented in its classic form. Many tried to improve it, but the design endured.
hook: Good enough can be unbeatable.

title: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
body: Inventors in 1957 tried to sell textured plastic as wallpaper. It failed, then found its use protecting fragile goods in shipping.
hook: Keep looking for the job your product does best.

title: Sunk costs trap good decision-makers
body: People keep investing in failing projects because of money already spent. The rational choice looks only at future costs and benefits.
hook: Past spending should not decide future spending.

title: A small loss feels bigger than an equal gain
body: Research by Kahneman and Tversky found losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as gains of the same size. This is called loss aversion.
hook: Framing a choice as a loss changes behaviour.

title: Ford's moving assembly line cut build time sharply
body: In 1913 Ford's moving line cut the time to build a Model T chassis from about 12 hours to around 90 minutes. Prices fell and sales soared.
hook: Process innovation can matter more than product.

title: IKEA's flat-pack idea started with a table leg
body: In the 1950s, an IKEA employee removed the legs from a table to fit it in a car. Flat-packing cut shipping and storage costs.
hook: Constraints can spark the best ideas.

title: Starbucks is named after a fictional character
body: The name comes from Starbuck, the first mate in Herman Melville's Moby-Dick. The founders wanted something evocative of the sea.
hook: Brands borrow stories.

title: The first online sale is often dated to 1994
body: In August 1994, a CD by Sting was sold online through a site called NetMarket, using encryption to protect the card details.
hook: Every giant market had a first customer.

title: Most of a company's value can be intangible
body: For many large listed firms, brands, software and patents make up most of the market value, not buildings or machines.
hook: The valuable stuff is often invisible.

title: Anchoring shapes negotiations
body: The first number mentioned in a negotiation tends to pull the final result towards it. Researchers call this anchoring.
hook: Going first can be an advantage.

title: Toyota's cars are built just in time
body: Toyota pioneered making parts only as they are needed. It cut waste and storage but made the company sensitive to supply shocks.
hook: Efficiency and resilience pull in opposite directions.

title: Kodak invented the digital camera
body: A Kodak engineer built a digital camera prototype in 1975. The company feared hurting its film business and was slow to embrace it.
hook: Protecting the old can block the new.

title: The first Apple logo showed Isaac Newton
body: Apple's 1976 logo was a detailed drawing of Newton sitting under an apple tree. It was soon replaced by the simpler apple.
hook: Simple usually wins in branding.

title: Gillette's razor model sells blades
body: Selling a cheap handle and profiting on replacement blades is known as the razor and blades model. Printers and coffee pods use it too.
hook: The profit is often in the refill.

title: Many banknotes contain cotton, not paper
body: US dollar notes are about 75 percent cotton and 25 percent linen. That makes them durable enough to survive the wash.
hook: Money is built to last.

title: The price of a Big Mac tracks currencies
body: The Economist's Big Mac Index compares burger prices to judge if currencies are over- or under-valued. It started as a light-hearted guide in 1986.
hook: Simple comparisons make complex ideas clear.

title: Rolex is owned by a charitable foundation
body: The Hans Wilsdorf Foundation owns Rolex. The founder set it up in 1945, and it holds the company today.
hook: Ownership structures can be unexpected.

title: McDonald's sells mostly through franchises
body: Most McDonald's restaurants are run by franchisees. The company earns rent and fees from them.
hook: Some businesses are property companies at heart.

title: Coffee is one of the most traded commodities
body: Coffee is grown in over 50 countries and traded worldwide. Millions of farmers depend on it for income.
hook: Your morning cup links to a global market.

title: Free trials often turn into subscriptions
body: Many people forget to cancel free trials. Firms count on this, which is why many countries now require clear reminders.
hook: Defaults drive behaviour.

title: The term "boycott" comes from a land agent
body: In 1880 Irish tenants refused to deal with Captain Charles Boycott. His name became the word for refusing to trade with someone.
hook: Collective action can make history.

title: Fax machines predate the telephone
body: Alexander Bain patented an early fax system in 1843, decades before the telephone was patented in 1876.
hook: Old ideas can wait for the right moment.

title: Supermarkets pipe in the smell of bread
body: Some stores use bakeries near the entrance so the smell of fresh bread greets shoppers. Pleasant smells can lift spending.
hook: Every sense can be used to sell.

title: The number of business days in a year is about 252
body: Stock markets are closed on weekends and holidays. That leaves about 252 trading days a year in the US.
hook: Finance runs on its own calendar.

title: Bitcoin's creator is unknown
body: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by someone using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. Their true identity has never been confirmed.
hook: Some of the biggest ideas are anonymous.

title: Branded goods often come from the same factory
body: Many supermarket own-brand products are made by the same manufacturers as big brands, sometimes on the same lines.
hook: The label can matter more than the product.

title: Loyalty schemes date back centuries
body: In the 1700s some American merchants gave customers copper tokens to redeem for later purchases. Stamps and points followed.
hook: Rewarding repeat business is timeless.

title: Companies can be older than countries
body: Some businesses, like Japan's Nishiyama Onsen Keiunkan inn founded in 705, are older than many modern nations.
hook: Businesses can outlive governments.

title: The Dutch East India Company issued the first public shares
body: Founded in 1602, it sold shares to the public and is often called the first publicly traded company.
hook: Modern finance has old roots.

title: Inflation means prices rise over time
body: If inflation is 2 percent a year, prices double in roughly 35 years. Savings that earn nothing slowly lose value.
hook: Standing still can mean falling behind.

title: Scarcity makes things seem more valuable
body: Studies found people rated cookies from a nearly empty jar as tastier than identical ones from a full jar.
hook: Limited supply sells.

title: Many famous brands started in garages
body: Garages are a classic start-up story because they are cheap and available. HP's original garage in Palo Alto is now a historic landmark.
hook: Start where you are with what you have.

title: Barcodes were inspired by Morse code
body: Inventor Norman Joseph Woodland reportedly drew Morse code dots and dashes in sand and stretched them into lines.
hook: Ideas borrow from other fields.

title: Price matching can reduce competition
body: When shops promise to match rivals' prices, competitors have less reason to cut prices. Economists debate the effect.
hook: A promise to customers can also signal to rivals.

title: Social proof drives sales
body: People are more likely to buy something if they see others doing it. Reviews, ratings and "bestseller" labels exploit this.
hook: We follow the crowd more than we think.

title: Most start-ups fail
body: Studies of start-ups suggest the majority do not survive a decade. Running out of money is a common reason.
hook: Survival is the first win.

title: Shipping costs used to dwarf product costs
body: Before containers, loading and unloading could be a huge share of the cost of trade. Containers cut that dramatically.
hook: Logistics can decide what is worth making.

title: Interest rates move house prices
body: When borrowing is cheap, buyers can afford bigger mortgages, which tends to push prices up. Higher rates can cool the market.
hook: Money's price affects every other price.

title: Coca-Cola's formula is a famous secret
body: The company keeps its recipe in a vault in Atlanta. The secrecy itself has become part of the marketing.
hook: Mystery can be a brand asset.

title: The 'paradox of choice' can stall buyers
body: In a famous study, shoppers offered 6 jams bought more than those offered 24. Too many options can make people walk away.
hook: Less choice can mean more sales.

title: The world's largest employer is not a company
body: Organisations like the US Department of Defense and China's People's Liberation Army employ millions. Walmart is among the largest private ones.
hook: Scale takes many forms.

title: A recession is often defined as two quarters of decline
body: A common rule of thumb calls two consecutive quarters of falling GDP a recession. Official bodies use broader measures.
hook: Simple rules help, but definitions vary.

title: Dynamic pricing changes by the minute
body: Airlines and ride apps adjust prices based on demand, time and other factors. The same seat can cost very different amounts.
hook: Price is a moving target.

title: Brand logos are often simplified over time
body: Many companies have flattened and simplified their logos to work on small screens and app icons.
hook: Design adapts to the medium.

title: Wrigley first sold soap and baking powder
body: William Wrigley Jr. gave away chewing gum as a bonus with his products. The gum became more popular, so he switched.
hook: Listen to what customers want.

title: The 'Veblen good' gets more desirable as it gets pricier
body: Some luxury goods sell better at higher prices because the price signals status. Economist Thorstein Veblen described this.
hook: Price can be part of the product.

title: The first company to hit a $1 trillion valuation was Apple
body: Apple reached a $1 trillion market value in August 2018. Others followed soon after.
hook: Big numbers become normal quickly.

title: Most money is digital
body: Physical cash makes up only a small share of the money supply in many economies. The rest exists as bank balances.
hook: Money is mostly information.

title: Credit scores date to the 1950s
body: The FICO company was founded in 1956. Its credit scoring became widespread in US lending later.
hook: Algorithms decided lending long before AI.

title: Patents last about 20 years
body: In most countries, a patent gives an inventor exclusive rights for around 20 years. After that, anyone can use the invention.
hook: Protection is temporary by design.

title: Long queues can attract more customers
body: A busy restaurant signals quality. Some places are said to keep queues outside even with free tables inside.
hook: Popularity can be self-fulfilling.

title: Moore's law guided chipmakers for decades
body: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted the number of transistors on a chip would keep doubling. The industry used it as a target.
hook: A prediction can become a plan.

title: Warranties are often profitable add-ons
body: Extended warranties sold at checkout can have high margins because many are never claimed.
hook: The extras can make the money.

title: Thinking in opportunity cost helps decisions
body: The cost of a choice includes the best alternative you give up. Spending an hour on one task means not spending it on another.
hook: Every yes is a no to something else.

title: Lego bricks from 1958 still fit today
body: Lego has kept the same basic stud-and-tube design since 1958, so old bricks connect with new ones.
hook: Compatibility builds loyalty.

title: The first commercial was a 10-second clock ad
body: In 1941 a Bulova watch ad aired on New York TV before a baseball game. It reportedly cost just a few dollars.
hook: Every giant ad industry started with a small slot.

title: Gift cards often go unspent
body: A share of gift card value is never redeemed. Retailers count some of that as profit, which is why they promote cards heavily.
hook: Unused value is still value to someone.

title: Hotels use a "rack rate"
body: The rack rate is a hotel's full published price. Few guests pay it, but it anchors discounts to look generous.
hook: A high reference price makes deals feel better.

title: Most cars are white, black, grey or silver
body: White, black, grey and silver dominate car sales worldwide because they are thought to hold resale value.
hook: Safe choices often win in big purchases.

title: Tipping customs vary widely
body: Tipping is expected in the US, modest in the UK, and can be seen as rude in Japan.
hook: Business rules are cultural.

title: Nintendo started by making playing cards
body: Founded in Kyoto in 1889, Nintendo produced hanafuda cards. It moved into toys and then video games much later.
hook: A company's first product rarely defines it.

title: Samsung once sold dried fish
body: Founded in 1938, Samsung began as a trading company dealing in groceries such as dried fish and noodles.
hook: Diversification can reshape a business entirely.

title: Unilever's Lifebuoy soap launched in 1894
body: Lever Brothers sold Lifebuoy as a hygiene soap in Victorian Britain. It is still sold in many countries today.
hook: Brands can outlast their founders by a century.

title: Trees can share nutrients underground
body: Fungal networks link the roots of many trees in a forest. Through them, trees can exchange water, carbon and nutrients, though how much and why is still debated.
hook: Forests are more connected than they look.

title: Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins
body: By slowing their heart rate, sloths can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes. Dolphins usually surface every 8 to 10 minutes.
hook: Slow living has hidden advantages.

title: Flamingos are pink because of their food
body: Flamingos are born grey. Pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat turn their feathers pink over time.
hook: You really are what you eat.

title: A group of crows is called a murder
body: The term dates back to the 15th century, when groups of animals were given poetic names. A group of owls is a parliament.
hook: Language preserves old superstitions.

title: Cows have best friends
body: Studies found cows show lower stress when paired with a preferred companion. They form close social bonds within herds.
hook: Social needs run deep across species.

title: Bamboo can grow almost a metre a day
body: Some bamboo species can grow up to about 90 centimetres in a single day. It is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
hook: Growth rates can be astonishing when conditions suit.

title: Sea otters hold hands while sleeping
body: Sea otters often float in groups called rafts and sometimes link paws so they do not drift apart. They also wrap themselves in kelp.
hook: Simple habits can solve hard problems.

title: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day
body: Eucalyptus leaves are low in nutrients and hard to digest. Koalas save energy by sleeping most of the day.
hook: Diet shapes daily life.

title: Some jellyfish can reverse ageing
body: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier life stage when stressed. In theory this cycle could repeat indefinitely.
hook: Nature bends rules we think are fixed.

title: Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror
body: Asian elephants have passed the mirror test, touching marks on their heads they could only see in a reflection. Few animals pass it.
hook: Self-awareness is not unique to humans.

title: Owls cannot move their eyes
body: Owl eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets. Instead, owls can turn their heads around 270 degrees.
hook: Limits often drive clever adaptations.

title: Bees communicate with a dance
body: Honeybees perform a waggle dance to tell others the direction and distance of food. The angle of the dance points relative to the Sun.
hook: Information can travel without words.

title: Hummingbirds cannot walk
body: Their feet are tiny and suited for perching, so they shuffle or fly even short distances. Their wings can beat dozens of times a second.
hook: Specialisation has trade-offs.

title: Penguins propose with pebbles
body: Male gentoo penguins search for smooth pebbles to offer females. Pebbles are used to build nests that keep eggs off cold ground.
hook: Courtship often has a practical side.

title: Tardigrades can survive in space
body: These tiny animals, under a millimetre long, survived exposure to the vacuum of space in a 2007 experiment. They can dry out and revive years later.
hook: Toughness comes in very small packages.

title: Crocodiles cannot stick out their tongues
body: A membrane holds a crocodile's tongue to the roof of its mouth. It helps stop water flowing into the throat when it opens its jaws underwater.
hook: Every feature has a reason.

title: The Amazon makes much of its own rain
body: Trees release huge amounts of water vapour through their leaves. This moisture forms clouds and rain over the forest and beyond.
hook: Ecosystems can create their own weather.

title: Seahorse fathers give birth
body: Female seahorses lay eggs in a pouch on the male, who carries them until they hatch. He then releases fully formed young.
hook: Parenting roles vary widely in nature.

title: Garden snails have thousands of teeth
body: A snail's tongue-like radula is covered in rows of tiny teeth, often numbering in the thousands. It scrapes food like a rasp, and worn teeth are replaced.
hook: Small creatures can carry surprising tools.

title: Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings
body: Uneven stiffness in a wombat's intestine shapes its droppings into cubes. They use them to mark territory on rocks and logs.
hook: Even odd details have a mechanism.

title: Giraffes have the same number of neck bones as you
body: Giraffes and humans both have seven neck vertebrae. Each of a giraffe's can be over 25 centimetres long.
hook: Evolution stretches a shared design.

title: Dolphins have names
body: Bottlenose dolphins develop signature whistles that work like names. Others use them to call specific individuals.
hook: Identity matters in social animals.

title: Mushrooms are closer to animals than plants
body: Genetic studies show fungi share a more recent common ancestor with animals than with plants. Like us, they cannot make food from sunlight.
hook: Appearances can mislead classification.

title: Snails can sleep for years
body: In dry conditions, some snails seal themselves in their shells and go dormant. They can stay that way for months, occasionally years.
hook: Waiting can be a survival skill.

title: Butterflies taste with their feet
body: Butterflies have taste receptors on their feet. Landing on a leaf tells a female whether it suits her caterpillars.
hook: Senses can be placed where they are most useful.

title: Polar bears have black skin
body: Under their white-looking fur, polar bears have black skin that absorbs heat. Their fur is actually transparent and hollow.
hook: Things are not always the colour they seem.

title: A woodpecker's tongue wraps around its skull
body: The tongue extends from the back of the mouth, around the skull, and helps cushion the brain from impact.
hook: Anatomy can be wildly inventive.

title: Some sharks must keep swimming to breathe
body: Species like the great white rely on water flowing over their gills as they swim. Others can pump water while resting.
hook: Not all sharks follow the same rule.

title: Arctic terns make the longest migrations
body: Arctic terns fly between the Arctic and Antarctic each year. Over a lifetime they may travel a distance equal to going to the Moon and back several times.
hook: Small birds can be extreme travellers.

title: Pigeons are smarter than their reputation
body: Experiments suggest pigeons can learn to distinguish images and even recognise objects in pictures. They are smarter than their reputation.
hook: Common animals can be underestimated.

title: Squirrels forget where they bury many nuts
body: Squirrels bury far more nuts than they eat. Forgotten ones can grow into new trees.
hook: Forgetfulness can plant forests.

title: Rats laugh when tickled
body: Researchers found rats make high-pitched chirps when tickled, which some interpret as a form of laughter.
hook: Joy may be more widespread than we think.

title: A snail can sleep while stuck to a wall
body: Snails rest in cycles, sometimes clinging to surfaces with dried mucus. They can stay attached for long periods.
hook: Rest takes many forms.

title: Kangaroos cannot walk backwards easily
body: Their large tails and powerful legs make backward movement very awkward. They are built to bound forward.
hook: Design shapes direction.

title: Starfish can regrow arms
body: Many starfish can regenerate lost arms. Some species can grow a whole new body from one arm if it contains part of the centre.
hook: Healing can be remarkable.

title: Hippos produce a reddish secretion
body: Hippos release an oily red fluid that acts like sunscreen and may protect against germs. It is sometimes called blood sweat but is neither.
hook: Names can mislead.

title: Leaves change colour as green fades
body: In autumn trees break down green chlorophyll. Yellow and orange pigments that were there all along show through.
hook: Some colours are always present, just hidden.

title: Elephants have a sensitive trunk
body: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can pick up a single peanut or lift heavy logs.
hook: Flexibility and strength can coexist.

title: Honeybees visit millions of flowers for a jar of honey
body: Making a single jar of honey can take bees around two million flower visits.
hook: Small efforts add up to sweet results.

title: Male lions sleep up to 20 hours a day
body: Lions save energy by resting most of the day. Hunting is short and intense.
hook: Rest is part of the strategy.

title: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals
body: Coral polyps build hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over thousands of years, they create reefs.
hook: Tiny builders can make huge structures.

title: Some birds use tools
body: New Caledonian crows shape twigs and leaves into hooks to pull insects from holes.
hook: Tool use is not unique to humans.

title: Moles can dig fast
body: A mole can dig several metres of tunnel in an hour. Its front paws are broad and powerful like shovels.
hook: Bodies are tools for a lifestyle.

title: Pandas spend most of the day eating
body: Giant pandas eat bamboo for around 10 to 16 hours a day. Bamboo is low in nutrients, so they need a lot.
hook: Diet shapes daily routine.

title: Earthworms improve soil
body: Earthworms mix soil and leave nutrient-rich casts. Charles Darwin spent years studying their importance.
hook: Small creatures can have big impacts.

title: Some fish can climb waterfalls
body: Certain Hawaiian gobies use suction-cup fins to climb high waterfalls to reach upstream habitats.
hook: Determination is not just human.

title: Deer grow new antlers each year
body: Male deer shed their antlers annually and grow a new set. Growing antler is among the fastest-growing animal tissue.
hook: Renewal can be built into life cycles.

title: The largest living thing may be a fungus
body: A honey fungus in Oregon spreads underground across nearly 10 square kilometres. It may be thousands of years old.
hook: The biggest things can be hidden.

title: Bats are the only mammals that truly fly
body: Some mammals glide, but bats are the only ones capable of powered flight. Their wings are stretched skin over long fingers.
hook: Evolution found a unique solution.

title: Chameleons change colour mainly to communicate
body: Colour changes often signal mood or territory rather than camouflage. They also help with temperature control.
hook: The obvious explanation is not always right.

title: Ducks have waterproof feathers
body: Ducks spread oil from a gland near their tails over their feathers. Tightly interlocking feathers also help keep water out.
hook: Maintenance keeps systems working.

title: Some plants can sense touch
body: The sensitive plant Mimosa pudica folds its leaves when touched. It may deter grazing animals.
hook: Plants are more responsive than they seem.

title: Owls fly almost silently
body: Special feather edges break up turbulence, letting owls approach prey with very little sound.
hook: Quiet design wins.

title: Goldfish have better memories than the myth
body: The "three-second memory" is a myth. Studies show goldfish can remember things for months.
hook: Popular sayings can be wrong.

title: Pigs are very intelligent
body: Pigs can learn tricks, solve puzzles and recognise individuals. Some studies compare them to dogs.
hook: Intelligence is widespread among animals.

title: Zebras' stripes may deter flies
body: Research suggests stripes confuse biting flies, making them less likely to land.
hook: Patterns can be practical.

title: A blue whale calf gains around 90 kilograms a day
body: Blue whale calves drink rich milk and grow very fast in their first months.
hook: Growth can be astonishing early on.

title: Spider silk is extremely strong for its weight
body: Some spider silk is stronger than steel of the same thickness and very stretchy.
hook: Nature makes high-performance materials.

title: Some trees communicate danger with chemicals
body: When attacked by insects, some trees release chemicals that may prompt nearby trees to boost their defences.
hook: Signals can travel through air.

title: Axolotls can regrow limbs
body: These Mexican salamanders can regenerate limbs, parts of the heart and even parts of the brain.
hook: Regeneration is a scientific puzzle.

title: Frogs drink through their skin
body: Most frogs absorb water through a patch of skin on their belly rather than drinking with their mouths.
hook: Bodies solve problems differently.

title: Peacock feathers get their colour from structure
body: The shimmering colours come from microscopic structures that reflect light, not pigments.
hook: Colour can be built, not dyed.

title: Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched
body: Female sea turtles often return to nest near where they were born, possibly guided by Earth's magnetic field.
hook: Some journeys come full circle.

title: Camels store fat, not water, in their humps
body: The hump stores fat for energy. Camels survive without water by conserving it efficiently.
hook: Myths often get the mechanism wrong.

title: Horses cannot vomit
body: A strong muscle at the entrance to a horse's stomach makes vomiting nearly impossible.
hook: Some bodies have one-way systems.

title: The mantis shrimp packs a fast punch
body: Its club-like limbs strike so fast they create bubbles that collapse with tiny shock waves. It can crack shells and glass.
hook: Speed is power.

title: Crows can hold grudges
body: Studies found crows remember faces of people who threatened them and warn others.
hook: Memory makes social animals smarter.

title: Bees can recognise human faces, some studies suggest
body: Experiments indicate honeybees can learn to tell apart images of faces.
hook: Even tiny brains can learn patterns.

title: Dragonflies are expert hunters
body: Dragonflies catch a very high share of prey they chase, among the most successful hunters known.
hook: Precision beats power.

title: Flamingos stand on one leg to save energy
body: Studies suggest standing on one leg takes less muscle effort for flamingos and may reduce heat loss.
hook: Strange postures can be efficient.

title: Male emperor penguins incubate eggs
body: Males balance eggs on their feet under a fold of skin through the Antarctic winter, fasting for weeks.
hook: Endurance can be parenting.

title: Some caterpillars mimic snakes
body: Certain caterpillars have markings that look like snake eyes, scaring off birds.
hook: Bluffing is a survival tactic.

title: Orcas are dolphins
body: Killer whales are the largest members of the dolphin family. They live in complex social groups.
hook: Names can hide family ties.

title: Grass grows from the base
body: Grass grows from near the ground, not the tips. That is why it survives grazing and mowing.
hook: Where you grow from determines how you recover.

title: Raccoons wash food, or seem to
body: Raccoons often dunk food in water. Scientists think it may heighten their sense of touch rather than clean it.
hook: Behaviour can have unexpected purposes.

title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
body: Their wings rotate at the shoulder, letting them hover and fly in any direction, including backwards.
hook: Flexibility opens new moves.

title: Sunflowers follow the Sun when young
body: Young sunflowers track the Sun from east to west. Mature flowers usually face east.
hook: Behaviour can change with age.

title: Cuttlefish can change texture as well as colour
body: They can alter skin colour and surface texture in moments to blend into surroundings.
hook: Disguise can be multi-dimensional.

title: The platypus lays eggs
body: The platypus is one of the few mammals that lays eggs. It also detects prey using electrical signals.
hook: Nature breaks its own rules.

title: Some ants farm fungus
body: Leafcutter ants cut leaves to feed fungus gardens, which they then eat. They have farmed for millions of years.
hook: Agriculture is older than humans.

title: Rainforests cover a small share of land
body: Tropical rainforests cover around 6 percent of Earth's land but hold a large share of its species.
hook: Small areas can hold great riches.

title: Koalas have fingerprints like humans
body: Koala fingerprints are so similar to ours that they can be hard to tell apart under a microscope.
hook: Evolution can repeat itself.

title: Some octopuses use coconut shells as shelter
body: Veined octopuses carry coconut halves and assemble them into shelters when needed.
hook: Planning ahead is not unique to us.

title: Snakes smell with their tongues
body: A snake flicks its tongue to collect scent particles and passes them to an organ in the roof of its mouth.
hook: Senses can be repurposed.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
body: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.
hook: Our idea of a day is only local.

title: There are more stars than grains of sand on Earth's beaches
body: Astronomers estimate around 10^22 to 10^24 stars in the observable universe. That likely outnumbers all the sand grains on Earth's beaches.
hook: Scale in space defeats intuition.

title: Footprints on the Moon could last millions of years
body: The Moon has no wind or rain to erase them. Unless a meteorite hits, the Apollo astronauts' bootprints will stay for a very long time.
hook: Without weather, history stays put.

title: Space is not completely silent to instruments
body: Sound cannot travel through the near-vacuum of space. But spacecraft record radio waves and plasma vibrations that scientists convert into sound.
hook: Translation reveals hidden signals.

title: Saturn would float in a big enough bath
body: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. In a hypothetical ocean large enough, it would float.
hook: Giant does not always mean heavy for its size.

title: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us
body: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. From the Sun to Earth, that takes around 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
hook: When you look at the sky, you see the past.

title: The International Space Station orbits every 90 minutes
body: The ISS travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. Astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.
hook: Speed changes even the rhythm of a day.

title: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system
body: Olympus Mons is about 22 kilometres high, more than twice the height of Everest above sea level. Its base is roughly the size of Poland.
hook: Low gravity lets mountains grow huge.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space
body: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can gain up to about 3 percent in height. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
hook: Gravity shapes our bodies every day.

title: A year on Neptune lasts 165 Earth years
body: Neptune is so far from the Sun that it takes about 165 years to complete one orbit. It completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.
hook: Distance stretches time.

title: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm
body: The storm is wider than Earth and has been observed for at least 150 years. It has been shrinking in recent decades.
hook: Some storms outlast centuries.

title: The Moon is slowly drifting away
body: Laser measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further from Earth each year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
hook: Tiny changes add up over billions of years.

title: You could fit all the planets between Earth and the Moon
body: The average Earth–Moon distance is about 384,400 kilometres. The diameters of all the other planets add up to slightly less than that.
hook: Space between things is vast.

title: Pluto is smaller than the Moon
body: Pluto's diameter is about 2,377 kilometres, while the Moon's is about 3,475. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
hook: Categories change as we learn more.

title: Mercury is not the hottest planet
body: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is beaten by Venus. Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping it above 460°C.
hook: Insulation matters more than distance.

title: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
body: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background put the age of the universe at roughly 13.8 billion years. Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
hook: We are newcomers in a very old story.

title: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object
body: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
hook: A message in a bottle, sent across the stars.

title: Some planets orbit two suns
body: Astronomers have found planets orbiting pairs of stars. Kepler-16b, found in 2011, was the first clear example.
hook: Science fiction keeps turning into science.

title: Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times a second
body: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radiation across space. The fastest known spin over 700 times a second.
hook: Collapse can create extreme spin.

title: There is a giant cloud of alcohol in space
body: Sagittarius B2, a gas cloud near the centre of our galaxy, contains large amounts of ethyl alcohol. It is spread too thin to be drinkable.
hook: Chemistry happens everywhere.

title: The Sun makes up 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass
body: All the planets, moons and asteroids together are a tiny fraction. Jupiter holds most of what is left.
hook: One giant dominates the family.

title: Black holes do not suck everything in
body: From a distance, a black hole's gravity behaves like any object of the same mass. Only very close in, past the event horizon, is escape impossible.
hook: Myths exaggerate the danger.

title: Mars has blue sunsets
body: Fine dust in the Martian atmosphere scatters blue light forward around the Sun. Rovers have photographed bluish sunsets.
hook: Different air paints a different sky.

title: A spoonful of the Sun's core would be scorching
body: The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius. Nuclear fusion there turns hydrogen into helium.
hook: Stars are nuclear furnaces.

title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
body: Earth's orbit is slightly oval. It reaches its closest point, perihelion, in early January, during northern winter.
hook: Seasons come from tilt, not distance.

title: The Moon has moonquakes
body: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded quakes on the Moon. Some shallow ones lasted for minutes.
hook: Even quiet worlds can shake.

title: There are more trees on Earth than stars in the Milky Way
body: Estimates put Earth's trees at around 3 trillion. The Milky Way holds roughly 100 to 400 billion stars.
hook: Our planet holds its own vast numbers.

title: Uranus spins on its side
body: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it rolls around the Sun. Each pole gets around 42 years of continuous sunlight.
hook: A single collision can change a planet forever.

title: The Sun is a middle-aged star
body: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old. It is expected to shine for roughly another 5 billion years.
hook: Our star is only halfway through its story.

title: Comets have two tails
body: A comet often has a curved dust tail and a straight ion tail. The ion tail always points away from the Sun.
hook: Solar wind shapes what we see.
