title: The Moon always shows the same face
body: The Moon spins once for every orbit of Earth, so the same side always faces us. This is called tidal locking.
hook: Gravity can sync rhythms.

title: The far side of the Moon is not dark
body: It gets as much sunlight as the near side. It was simply unseen until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959.
hook: Hidden is not the same as dark.

title: Space smells, according to astronauts
body: Astronauts have described a smell like seared steak or hot metal on their suits after spacewalks.
hook: Space has a scent, even without air.

title: Mars has two small moons
body: Phobos and Deimos are small and irregular. Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards and may break apart in tens of millions of years.
hook: Even moons have lifespans.

title: The Milky Way will merge with Andromeda
body: In about 4 to 5 billion years, our galaxy and Andromeda are expected to collide and merge. Stars are so far apart they rarely hit each other.
hook: Even collisions can be peaceful at scale.

title: Jupiter has the most massive moon system
body: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury.
hook: Some moons outsize planets.

title: Saturn's rings are mostly ice
body: The rings are made largely of water ice chunks, from tiny grains to boulders. They are very wide but often only tens of metres thick.
hook: Huge structures can be incredibly thin.

title: A light year measures distance, not time
body: It is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
hook: Some words trick us with their names.

title: The first animal in orbit was a dog
body: Laika orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957. She did not survive the mission.
hook: Progress has had real costs.

title: Astronauts lose bone mass in space
body: Without gravity, bones lose density. Astronauts exercise for about two hours a day to limit the loss.
hook: Gravity keeps us strong.

title: Venus is the hottest planet
body: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping surface temperatures around 465°C.
hook: Atmosphere can matter more than distance.

title: Mercury has ice
body: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury may have water ice in shadowed craters at its poles.
hook: Extremes can sit side by side.

title: The Sun is mostly hydrogen
body: By mass, the Sun is about 73 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium, with traces of other elements.
hook: Stars are built from the simplest stuff.

title: There may be a planet with diamond rain
body: Scientists think the extreme pressures inside Neptune and Uranus may turn carbon into diamonds that sink like rain.
hook: Weather can be stranger than fiction.

title: Shooting stars are tiny
body: Most meteors are grains of dust or sand that burn up in the atmosphere. They glow because they hit the air at huge speed.
hook: Small things can make big displays.

title: Earth gets heavier from space dust
body: Tens of thousands of tonnes of cosmic dust fall on Earth every year.
hook: The sky is always falling, slowly.

title: Pluto has a heart
body: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft found a huge heart-shaped region of nitrogen ice on Pluto in 2015.
hook: Distant worlds can surprise us.

title: Olympus Mons would be hard to see from its base
body: It is so broad that its slopes curve away over the horizon. From the base you could not see the summit.
hook: Scale can make giants invisible.

title: The ISS is visible from the ground
body: The International Space Station often looks like a bright, steady star moving across the sky.
hook: You can watch people living in space.

title: There is no up or down in space
body: In orbit, astronauts float freely and arrange equipment on every surface.
hook: Orientation is just a convention.

title: The Sun's light is white
body: The Sun gives off all colours of visible light, which combine to white. It looks yellow because of our atmosphere.
hook: The sky changes how we see.

title: Mars has seasons
body: Mars is tilted like Earth, so it has seasons. They last about twice as long because its year is longer.
hook: Familiar patterns appear on other worlds.

title: Europa may have an ocean
body: Jupiter's moon Europa is thought to have a salty ocean beneath its icy crust. It is a target in the search for life.
hook: Life may hide under ice.

title: The asteroid belt is mostly empty
body: Asteroids are far apart, often hundreds of thousands of kilometres. Spacecraft fly through without trouble.
hook: Sci-fi crowds space too much.

title: A spacesuit is like a personal spacecraft
body: It provides oxygen, pressure, temperature control and protection from radiation and dust.
hook: Survival needs a lot of kit.

title: We have only seen one side of the Milky Way
body: Because we are inside it, we cannot photograph the whole galaxy. Pictures of it are illustrations or other galaxies.
hook: Some views are impossible from inside.

title: Solar eclipses happen by coincidence
body: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times further away. So they look the same size.
hook: A cosmic coincidence gives us eclipses.

title: Saturn's moon Titan has lakes
body: Titan has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane. It also has rain and a thick atmosphere.
hook: Familiar landscapes can form from alien stuff.

title: The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin
body: On 12 April 1961, Gagarin orbited Earth once in Vostok 1. The flight lasted about 108 minutes.
hook: One orbit changed the world.

title: Twelve people have walked on the Moon
body: Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo missions.
hook: A small club with a giant achievement.

title: Space is cold, but not everywhere
body: In shadow, objects can get extremely cold. In direct sunlight they can get very hot, so spacecraft need thermal control.
hook: Extremes depend on where you stand.

title: The Andromeda galaxy is visible without a telescope
body: On a dark night it looks like a faint smudge. It is about 2.5 million light years away.
hook: You can see another galaxy with your own eyes.

title: The Moon makes Earth's tides
body: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating bulges. The Sun contributes too, making spring and neap tides.
hook: Distant objects shape our daily lives.

title: Earth's magnetic field protects us
body: It deflects much of the solar wind. Without it, our atmosphere could slowly be stripped away.
hook: Invisible shields matter.

title: Auroras are caused by the solar wind
body: Charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, making the sky glow.
hook: Space weather paints the sky.

title: Black holes can spin
body: Many black holes rotate, some at close to the maximum possible speed. Spin affects how matter falls in.
hook: Even the darkest objects move.

title: The Kármán line marks where space begins
body: It is commonly set at 100 kilometres above sea level. Some organisations use 80 kilometres instead.
hook: Boundaries are often agreed, not natural.

title: Space junk is a growing problem
body: Thousands of defunct satellites and fragments orbit Earth. Collisions can create more debris.
hook: Every launch leaves a trace.

title: The first image of a black hole came in 2019
body: The Event Horizon Telescope linked telescopes worldwide to image the black hole in galaxy M87.
hook: Teamwork can see the invisible.

title: Hubble has been in orbit since 1990
body: The Hubble Space Telescope has made over a million observations. It was repaired by astronauts several times.
hook: Maintenance can extend a mission for decades.

title: Light from the Moon is reflected sunlight
body: The Moon makes no light of its own. It reflects only around 12 percent of the sunlight that hits it.
hook: Even brightness can be borrowed.

title: A day on Mars is about 24 hours 40 minutes
body: A Martian day is called a sol. Rover teams on Earth have worked on Mars time.
hook: Some alien rhythms feel familiar.

title: Stars come in many colours
body: Hotter stars look blue-white, cooler ones look red. The Sun is a medium-temperature yellow-white star.
hook: Colour reveals temperature.

title: Jupiter protects Earth, partly
body: Its gravity can deflect some comets and asteroids, though it can also send others towards the inner solar system.
hook: Big neighbours have mixed effects.

title: Most of the universe is invisible
body: Ordinary matter makes up only about 5 percent of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy.
hook: We understand only a small slice.

title: Space has a speed record holder
body: NASA's Parker Solar Probe became the fastest human-made object, travelling hundreds of thousands of kilometres per hour near the Sun.
hook: Gravity can be a slingshot.

title: The Moon formed from a collision, most likely
body: The leading theory says a Mars-sized body hit early Earth, and debris formed the Moon.
hook: Violent beginnings can create beauty.

title: Spacecraft use gravity assists
body: Probes swing past planets to gain speed and change direction without extra fuel.
hook: Clever paths save energy.

title: Galaxies come in shapes
body: Astronomers classify galaxies as spiral, elliptical or irregular. The Milky Way is a barred spiral.
hook: Patterns help us understand the vast.

title: The Sun loses mass every second
body: Through fusion and solar wind, the Sun loses millions of tonnes of mass each second. It has plenty to spare.
hook: Even giants spend.

title: Astronauts' voices sound normal inside the station
body: The ISS is filled with air, so sound travels as normal. Only in the vacuum outside is there silence.
hook: Silence needs a vacuum.

title: Exoplanets number in the thousands
body: Over 5,000 planets outside our solar system have been confirmed. Many more are likely.
hook: Planets are common.

title: Venus has no moons
body: Venus and Mercury are the only planets in our solar system without moons.
hook: Not every planet has company.

title: The Great Bear is not a constellation's full story
body: The Plough, or Big Dipper, is part of the larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.
hook: Familiar shapes can be pieces of bigger pictures.

title: "Salary" may come from salt
body: The word comes from the Latin "salarium". A popular story says Roman soldiers were paid in salt, though historians say the link is uncertain.
hook: Good stories cling to words.

title: "Goodbye" means "God be with you"
body: The word is a contraction of the 16th-century phrase "God be with ye". Over time it shortened, influenced by "good day".
hook: Everyday words hide old sentences.

title: "Nice" used to mean foolish
body: In Middle English, "nice" meant silly or ignorant, from the Latin "nescius". Its meaning shifted many times before becoming "pleasant".
hook: Words can flip their meaning entirely.

title: "Quarantine" comes from forty days
body: In 14th-century Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before landing. The Italian "quaranta giorni" means forty days.
hook: Public health shaped our vocabulary.

title: English has no official regulator
body: Unlike French, which has the Académie française, English has no official body deciding its rules. Dictionaries record usage rather than dictate it.
hook: English grows by use, not decree.

title: "Robot" comes from a Czech play
body: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced the word. It comes from "robota", meaning forced labour.
hook: Fiction often names the future.

title: The dot over an i is called a tittle
body: The small mark over a lowercase i or j is a tittle. It is thought to be where the phrase "to a T" may come from, though that is debated.
hook: Tiny things have names too.

title: "Muscle" means little mouse
body: It comes from the Latin "musculus", little mouse. Romans thought flexing muscles looked like mice moving under the skin.
hook: Body words are full of animal pictures.

title: "Disaster" means bad star
body: It comes from the Italian "disastro", from "dis" (bad) and "astro" (star). Disasters were once blamed on the stars.
hook: Superstition lives on in vocabulary.

title: "Clue" comes from a ball of thread
body: A "clew" was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus used thread to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clew became something that guides you.
hook: Myths become metaphors, then words.

title: Shakespeare is credited with many new words
body: Words like "lonely", "swagger" and "bedroom" first appear in print in his works. Some may simply have been recorded first by him.
hook: First written is not always first said.

title: "OK" started as a joke
body: In 1839, Boston newspapers had a fad for comic abbreviations. "OK" stood for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of "all correct".
hook: Jokes can become global words.

title: Hawaiian has a 13-letter alphabet
body: The Hawaiian alphabet uses five vowels and eight consonants, including the ʻokina glottal stop. Words often repeat sounds.
hook: Small alphabets can carry rich languages.

title: "Sabotage" may come from shoes
body: One theory says it comes from the French "sabot", a wooden clog, linked to workers clumping or disrupting work. The exact origin is debated.
hook: Etymology is often a best guess.

title: "Avocado" comes from an Aztec word
body: The Nahuatl word "āhuacatl" was adapted by Spanish speakers into "aguacate", which became "avocado" in English.
hook: Food words carry trade history.

title: The longest English word in major dictionaries is a lung disease
body: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis has 45 letters. It was coined in 1935, partly to be the longest word.
hook: Some words exist just to be records.

title: "Bless you" is said in many languages
body: Many cultures have a response to sneezing, such as "Gesundheit" in German, meaning health. The customs probably grew from wishing good health.
hook: Small rituals unite cultures.

title: "Handicap" came from a betting game
body: "Hand in cap" was a 17th-century trading game. It later described evening out horse races, then disadvantages in general.
hook: Words travel far from their origins.

title: "Ketchup" may come from a fish sauce
body: One theory traces it to a Hokkien Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce. Tomatoes were added much later.
hook: Recipes and words both evolve.

title: Some languages have no words for left and right
body: Guugu Yimithirr in Australia uses compass directions instead, such as north and south. Speakers keep a constant sense of orientation.
hook: Language can shape how we think about space.

title: "Alphabet" comes from its first two letters
body: It comes from Greek "alpha" and "beta", the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. The Greeks adapted them from Phoenician letters.
hook: Names often describe their beginnings.

title: "Hazard" came from a dice game
body: "Hazard" was a medieval dice game, likely from an Arabic word for dice. The meaning shifted from chance to danger.
hook: Risk and games share roots.

title: The ampersand was once a letter
body: "&" comes from a ligature of "et", Latin for "and". Children once recited it at the end of the alphabet as "and per se and".
hook: Symbols can be worn-down words.

title: "Deadline" was once a real line
body: In the American Civil War, a deadline was a boundary in some prison camps that prisoners could not cross. Later it moved into printing and journalism.
hook: Some everyday words have dark origins.

title: Mandarin uses tones to change meaning
body: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold, depending on its tone. There are four main tones plus a neutral one.
hook: Pitch can carry meaning.

title: "Lord" once meant loaf-keeper
body: It comes from the Old English "hlafweard", meaning guardian of the loaf. "Lady" comes from "hlæfdige", loaf-kneader.
hook: Power once meant controlling the bread.

title: "Bankrupt" comes from a broken bench
body: It is linked to the Italian "banca rotta", meaning broken bench. Moneylenders worked at benches, and a broken one signalled failure.
hook: Business failure has a vivid history.

title: "Bedlam" comes from a hospital
body: Bethlem Royal Hospital in London, a psychiatric hospital, was nicknamed Bedlam. The word came to mean chaos.
hook: Place names can turn into everyday words.

title: "Sincere" might mean without wax
body: A popular story says it means "without wax", from sculptors hiding flaws. Most scholars trace it to Latin "sincerus", meaning pure.
hook: Charming etymologies are often wrong.

title: "Tragedy" may mean goat song
body: It comes from the Greek "tragōidia", possibly from "tragos", goat, and "ōidē", song. Why goats is still debated.
hook: Some origins remain mysterious.

title: "Window" means wind eye
body: It comes from the Old Norse "vindauga", combining wind and eye.
hook: Words can be little poems.

title: "Nightmare" involves a goblin, not a horse
body: The "mare" in nightmare comes from an Old English word for a spirit that sat on sleepers' chests.
hook: Similar sounds can hide different meanings.

title: "Daisy" means day's eye
body: It comes from Old English "dægesēage", because the flower opens in the morning and closes at night.
hook: Names can describe behaviour.

title: "Pupil" means little doll
body: The pupil of the eye comes from Latin "pupilla", little doll, after the tiny reflection you see of yourself in someone's eye.
hook: Small observations shape words.

title: "Companion" means bread-sharer
body: From Latin "com", with, and "panis", bread. A companion is someone you share bread with.
hook: Friendship begins at the table.

title: "Sarcasm" means to tear flesh
body: It comes from the Greek "sarkazein", to tear flesh, later meaning to sneer.
hook: Words can bite.

title: "Hello" became popular with the telephone
body: Thomas Edison is credited with promoting "hello" as a telephone greeting. Alexander Graham Bell preferred "ahoy".
hook: Technology can choose our words.

title: "Emoji" is not related to emotion
body: It comes from Japanese "e", picture, and "moji", character. The resemblance to "emotion" is a coincidence.
hook: Coincidences shape how words feel.

title: "Panic" comes from the god Pan
body: Pan was a Greek god of the wild, said to cause sudden fear in travellers.
hook: Gods live on in our vocabulary.

title: "Cereal" comes from a goddess
body: It comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.
hook: Breakfast has divine origins.

title: "Jeans" may come from Genoa
body: The cloth is linked to Genoa in Italy, called "Gênes" in French. Denim comes from "de Nîmes", a French town.
hook: Clothes carry place names.

title: "Tuxedo" comes from a place
body: It is named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where the jacket became fashionable in the 1880s.
hook: Fashion travels with names.

title: "Quiz" has a disputed origin
body: A famous story says it was invented for a bet in Dublin. Historians find no evidence and the real origin is unclear.
hook: Some origin stories are too good to be true.

title: "Silly" once meant blessed
body: In Old English, "sælig" meant happy or blessed. Over centuries it shifted to innocent, then foolish.
hook: Meanings can drift a long way.

title: "Awful" once meant full of awe
body: It originally meant inspiring wonder or fear. It now usually means very bad.
hook: Words can lose their sparkle.

title: "Mortgage" means death pledge
body: It comes from Old French "mort", dead, and "gage", pledge. The pledge dies when the debt is paid or the property is taken.
hook: Finance has gloomy roots.

title: "Girl" once meant any young person
body: In Middle English, "gyrle" could refer to a young person of either sex.
hook: Words can narrow over time.

title: "Pedigree" comes from a crane's foot
body: It comes from French "pied de grue", crane's foot, because family tree lines looked like a bird's foot.
hook: Diagrams can name ideas.

title: "Algebra" comes from Arabic
body: It comes from "al-jabr", from the title of a 9th-century book by the mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
hook: Maths carries history in its words.

title: "Algorithm" comes from a person's name
body: It derives from al-Khwarizmi, whose name was Latinised as Algoritmi.
hook: People can become concepts.

title: "Checkmate" means the king is helpless
body: It comes from Persian "shāh māt", often translated as "the king is helpless" or "the king is stuck".
hook: Games carry language across continents.

title: "Hippopotamus" means river horse
body: It comes from the Greek "hippos", horse, and "potamos", river.
hook: Names can be descriptions.

title: "Pineapple" once meant pine cone
body: In English, "pineapple" first meant a pine cone. The tropical fruit took the name because of its resemblance.
hook: Names get recycled.

title: "Coffee" travelled through many languages
body: It came via Dutch "koffie" from Turkish "kahve", from Arabic "qahwa".
hook: A word can journey as far as the bean.

title: "Ketchup" spellings once varied
body: Catsup and catchup were common spellings. Ketchup became standard over the 20th century.
hook: Spelling can be settled by markets.

title: "Serendipity" comes from a fairy tale
body: Horace Walpole coined it in 1754, after the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip.
hook: Lucky discoveries got a lucky name.

title: "Nerd" may come from Dr Seuss
body: The word appears in Dr Seuss's 1950 book If I Ran the Zoo. Its later slang use spread from the US.
hook: Children's books can coin words.

title: "Gaslighting" comes from a play
body: It comes from the 1938 play Gas Light and its film versions, where a husband manipulates his wife.
hook: Stories give names to experiences.

title: "Spam" email is named after a sketch
body: Monty Python's 1970 sketch has a café where Spam is in everything. The repetition inspired the name for junk messages.
hook: Comedy names technology.

title: "Bluetooth" is named after a king
body: It is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united tribes, as the technology unites devices.
hook: Brands borrow from history.

title: "Google" comes from googol
body: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros. The company's name is a playful misspelling.
hook: A typo can become a giant brand.

title: "Lol" is in the Oxford English Dictionary
body: "LOL" was added to the OED in 2011. Internet language now shapes mainstream English.
hook: Dictionaries follow usage.

title: English borrows from many languages
body: Around 80 percent of English vocabulary is estimated to be borrowed. Latin and French gave large shares.
hook: English is a magpie language.

title: "Schadenfreude" has no single English word
body: German combines "Schaden", harm, and "Freude", joy, to mean pleasure at others' misfortune.
hook: Some languages name feelings others cannot.

title: "Hygge" became a lifestyle trend
body: The Danish word for cosiness and contentment became popular in English around 2016.
hook: Words can export a way of life.

title: The most common letter in English is E
body: E appears in English text more than any other letter, around 12 percent of the time.
hook: Patterns help codebreakers.

title: "Q" is almost always followed by "U"
body: In English words, Q is nearly always followed by U. Exceptions often come from other languages, like "qi".
hook: Rules have exceptions, often borrowed.

title: Some words are their own opposites
body: "Sanction" can mean allow or penalise. "Dust" can mean remove dust or add it. These are called contronyms.
hook: Context decides meaning.

title: "Bookkeeper" has three double letters in a row
body: It has oo, kk and ee consecutively. "Bookkeeping" does too.
hook: Spelling holds puzzles.

title: "Strengths" has one vowel
body: The nine-letter word has just one vowel. It is one of the longest English words like that.
hook: Consonants can carry a word.

title: "Set" has a huge number of meanings
body: The Oxford English Dictionary lists hundreds of senses for "set", though "run" has overtaken it in some counts.
hook: Small words do heavy lifting.

title: Pangrams use every letter
body: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" contains every letter of the alphabet. It was used to test typewriters.
hook: Clever sentences have practical jobs.

title: The dot-com era gave us new words
body: Words like "email", "website" and "download" became everyday English in the 1990s.
hook: Technology rapidly reshapes language.

title: Japanese has three writing systems
body: Japanese uses kanji, hiragana and katakana, often together in a single sentence.
hook: Writing can mix systems.

title: Finnish has 15 grammatical cases
body: Finnish nouns change form in many ways to express meaning that English shows with prepositions.
hook: Grammar takes many forms.

title: Some languages have no word for blue
body: Several languages historically used one word for both blue and green. Linguists call this "grue".
hook: Colour vocabulary varies widely.

title: Sign languages are full languages
body: British Sign Language and American Sign Language are distinct, each with its own grammar.
hook: Language is not only spoken.

title: The word "the" is the most common in English
body: "The" is the most frequently used word in written English.
hook: The smallest words do the most work.

title: "Okay" is one of the most widely understood words
body: OK is used and understood in many languages around the world.
hook: A joke abbreviation went global.

title: "Cockney rhyming slang" hides meanings
body: "Apples and pears" means stairs, and often only the first word is used: "up the apples".
hook: Slang can be a secret code.

title: "Avocado" and "guacamole" share a root
body: Both trace back to the Nahuatl "āhuacatl". Guacamole adds "mōlli", meaning sauce.
hook: Food words travel together.

title: "Trivia" means three roads
body: From Latin "trivium", where three roads meet. Gossip at crossroads came to mean small, everyday matters.
hook: Small talk has a street address.

title: "Ciao" once meant your servant
body: The Italian greeting comes from the Venetian "s'ciavo", meaning I am your servant.
hook: Politeness can wear down into a casual hello.

title: "Curfew" means cover the fire
body: From Old French "cuevrefeu", a medieval signal to cover hearth fires for the night.
hook: Safety rules leave traces in language.
